cases.name: Zulueta v. Court of Appeals
cases.subject: Mercantile Law
cases.facts: Cecilia Zulueta is the wife of Dr. Alfredo Martin. On March 26, 1982, she entered her husband's medical clinic and, in the presence of her mother, a driver, and his secretary, forcibly opened the drawers and cabinet there. She took 157 documents and papers: private letters between Dr. Martin and his alleged mistresses, greeting cards, cancelled checks, diaries, his passport, and photographs. She wanted to use them as evidence in the case she had filed against him for legal separation and for disqualification from practicing medicine. Dr. Martin sued to get the papers back and for damages. The trial court ruled for him, ordered her to return the papers, made her pay damages, and barred her and her lawyers from using the papers as evidence. The Court of Appeals agreed. Zulueta's only argument before the Supreme Court was that in an earlier disbarment case against her lawyer (Martin v. Felix, Jr.), the Court had already ruled these papers admissible as evidence.
cases.issue: Are the papers that the wife took from her husband's clinic, without his knowledge and consent, admissible as evidence, on the theory that the Court already held them admissible in the earlier disbarment case against her lawyer?
cases.ruling: No. The petition was denied. (1) The earlier case did not decide that the papers were admissible. The lawyer was cleared in that case only because, when he used the papers, the trial court's order banning their use was temporarily stopped by the Supreme Court's restraining order (TRO). Once that TRO was lifted, the ban applied again. (2) The papers are inadmissible. The Constitution says the privacy of communication and correspondence is inviolable, and this applies even when the person who violated it is the wife. The only exceptions are a lawful order of the court, or when public safety or order requires otherwise, as prescribed by law. Evidence obtained in violation of this is inadmissible for any purpose in any proceeding. (3) Marriage does not take away a person's right to privacy. The intimacies between husband and wife do not justify either one breaking into the other's drawers and cabinets to look for evidence of infidelity. The law protects free communication between spouses by making it privileged, but freedom of communication is different from forcing each spouse to share everything they know with the other. **A wife's taking of her husband's private papers violated his privacy of communication; the papers were inadmissible.**
cases.keyDoctrine: The constitutional right to privacy of communication and correspondence (1987 Constitution, Art. III, Sec. 3) applies even between husband and wife. Evidence obtained in violation of it is inadmissible for any purpose in any proceeding. The only exceptions are a lawful order of the court, or when public safety or order requires otherwise, as prescribed by law. A person does not give up their right to privacy by getting married.

cases.name: Spouses Hing v. Choachuy, Sr.
cases.subject: Mercantile Law
cases.facts: Spouses Bill and Victoria Hing own a lot in Mandaue City, Cebu. Next to it is a building of Aldo Development & Resources, Inc. (Aldo), where an auto-repair shop operates. Aldo had earlier sued the Hings, claiming their fence construction would destroy its wall, but that court denied Aldo's request for an injunction (a court order to stop an act) for lack of proof. The Hings then sued Alexander Choachuy, Sr. and Allan Choachuy. They said that, to gather evidence for Aldo's case, the Choachuys installed two video surveillance cameras on Aldo's building facing the Hings' property, and had employees take pictures of the Hings' construction without consent. The Choachuys said they did not install the cameras and were only stockholders of Aldo, not its owners. After an ocular inspection (the judge visited and viewed the site), the trial court ordered them to remove a revolving camera that viewed the Hings' lot and move it elsewhere. The Court of Appeals annulled that order. It reasoned that the Civil Code's protection of the privacy of one's residence did not apply because the property was not used as a residence, and that the Choachuys, as mere stockholders, could not have installed the cameras.
cases.issue: (1) Did installing surveillance cameras facing the Hings' property violate their right to privacy, even though the property was not used as a residence? (2) Were the Choachuys the proper parties to be sued, even though Aldo, not they, owned the building?
cases.ruling: The petition was granted and the trial court's injunction was reinstated. (1) Yes, there was a violation. The right to privacy is simply 'the right to be let alone.' Article 26(1) of the Civil Code forbids prying into the privacy of another's residence, but it also covers 'similar acts.' Following Tolentino, a business office is entitled to the same privacy when the public is excluded and only allowed persons may enter. So the protection covers places, locations, or even situations a person considers private, as long as society recognizes that right. Courts use the 'reasonable expectation of privacy' test, a two-part test: (a) did the person, by their conduct, show an expectation of privacy; and (b) is that expectation one society recognizes as reasonable. This is decided case by case. Surveillance cameras should not cover places where there is a reasonable expectation of privacy unless the affected person consents, and should not be used to pry into another's residence or business office, which would be no different from eavesdropping, a crime under R.A. No. 4200 (Anti-Wiretapping Law). The Hings had a reasonable expectation of privacy in their property, whether used as a business office or residence, so cameras facing it or covering a significant part of it without their consent clearly violated their privacy. (2) Yes, the Choachuys were proper parties. Not owning the building does not mean they did not cause the cameras to be installed. Aldo is a family corporation managed by the Choachuy family, there was a long-running boundary dispute between the two families, and the Choachuys let the court inspect the building and argued that Aldo would be damaged if the cameras were moved. They were using Aldo's separate corporate personality as a shield.
cases.keyDoctrine: The right to privacy under Article 26(1) of the Civil Code is not limited to a residence. It extends to places where a person has the right to exclude the public, like a business office. Whether privacy was violated is decided by the 'reasonable expectation of privacy' test: (1) did the person, by their conduct, show an expectation of privacy, and (2) is that expectation one society recognizes as reasonable. Surveillance cameras may not cover places where there is a reasonable expectation of privacy without the affected person's consent.

cases.name: Vivares v. St. Theresa's College
cases.subject: Mercantile Law
cases.facts: Julia and Julienne, both minors, were graduating high school students at St. Theresa's College (STC) in Cebu City. In January 2012, while changing into swimsuits for a beach party, they and others took pictures of themselves in their undergarments. Another student, Angela, uploaded the pictures to her Facebook profile. Escudero, an STC computer teacher, learned about the photos from her students. Using STC's computers, those students logged into their own Facebook accounts and showed her more photos of the girls, including photos of them drinking and smoking in a bar and walking the streets in clothes that showed their brassieres. The students said that at times these photos were viewable by any Facebook user. Escudero reported this to STC's discipline officer. STC found that the girls broke the Student Handbook and barred them from the graduation ceremony. Julia's mother (Vivares) and Julienne's parents (the Suzaras) then filed a petition for a writ of habeas data (a court remedy to protect a person's information privacy). They said the girls' Facebook accounts were set to 'Friends Only,' that Escudero intruded into the accounts and saved and showed the photos without consent, and that STC spread them by attaching them to its court papers in a related case. The trial court dismissed the petition.
cases.issue: Should a writ of habeas data be issued? More specifically, was there an actual or threatened violation of the minors' right to privacy when STC viewed and used the Facebook photos?
cases.ruling: No. The petition was denied. (1) Procedural points: The writ of habeas data is not limited to cases of extralegal killings and enforced disappearances. It is an independent remedy to enforce the right to informational privacy. Also, the person or entity sued need not be in the business of gathering data. To be 'engaged' in gathering, collecting, or storing data just means doing or taking part in it. (2) The right to informational privacy is the right of individuals to control information about themselves. Having an expectation of privacy is not incompatible with using online social networks (OSNs) like Facebook. But a user must first show the intention to keep a post private by using the OSN's privacy tools. Using these tools is how a person claims informational privacy online. (3) Here, the girls did not prove they limited who could see the photos. Their claim that only five people could see them was self-serving. They did not dispute that the girls' Facebook friends showed the photos using their own accounts, with no special means. Since Facebook's default setting is 'Public,' the photos may be presumed viewable by everyone. Even a 'Friends Only' setting does not make a post very private, because friends can share posts or tag others, which widens the audience. STC officials were mere recipients of photos voluntarily shown by people who had legitimate access to them. They used no unlawful means, and attaching the photos to court papers was not a privacy violation. The result might have been different if the photos had been set to 'Only Me' or a 'Custom' list. (4) On cyber responsibility: internet users must be careful and use privacy tools if they want to keep information private. The Court cannot protect people who did nothing to put the matter within their private zone.
cases.keyDoctrine: The right to informational privacy is the right to control information about oneself. A social media user has a reasonable expectation of privacy only if they show the intention to keep a post private by using the platform's privacy tools to limit who can see it. A 'Public' or even 'Friends Only' post is not automatically private. A writ of habeas data needs proof, at least by substantial evidence, of an actual or threatened violation of the right to privacy in life, liberty, or security. It is not limited to extralegal killings and enforced disappearances.

cases.name: Cadajas v. People
cases.subject: Mercantile Law
cases.facts: Christian Cadajas, 24, met AAA, 14, at the canteen where he worked. They chatted on Facebook Messenger and became sweethearts in April 2016. AAA's mother, BBB, learned of the relationship because AAA used BBB's phone to access her Facebook account and sometimes forgot to log out. BBB disapproved and told Cadajas to stay away because AAA was a minor. In November 2016, BBB read messages in which Cadajas coaxed AAA into sending him photos of her breasts and vagina, which AAA did. AAA rushed to a computer shop to delete the messages, but BBB forced her to open Cadajas's Facebook Messenger account (AAA had his password) to get a copy of the conversation. Cadajas was charged with child pornography under Section 4(c)(2) of R.A. No. 10175 (Cybercrime Prevention Act), in relation to R.A. No. 9775 (Anti-Child Pornography Act). The trial court convicted him, and the Court of Appeals affirmed. Before the Supreme Court, he argued that the photos and messages were inadmissible because they were taken from his Facebook Messenger account in violation of his right to privacy.
cases.issue: (1) Were the photos and messages taken from Cadajas's Facebook Messenger account inadmissible because they were obtained in violation of his right to privacy? (2) Was he guilty of child pornography committed through a computer system?
cases.ruling: The petition was denied, and the penalty was increased to reclusion perpetua. (1) The evidence was admissible. The constitutional rule that evidence obtained in violation of the privacy of communication is inadmissible (Art. III, Sec. 3) protects people against the government, not against other private individuals. Here the evidence was obtained by a private person, not by the police or any agent of the State. The Court said its statement in Zulueta v. Court of Appeals about inadmissibility between spouses was a mere obiter dictum (a side remark that is not a binding precedent). Privacy violations between private individuals are governed by the Civil Code, the Data Privacy Act, and other laws, and admissibility is governed by the Rules on Evidence. The evidence was properly authenticated when AAA identified it in court. The Data Privacy Act also allows processing of sensitive personal information when it relates to determining criminal liability, or when necessary to protect lawful rights in court proceedings. Applying the 'reasonable expectation of privacy' test from Spouses Hing v. Choachuy, Sr., there was no privacy violation: Cadajas voluntarily gave AAA his password, which limited his expectation of privacy as to her. It does not matter that her mother forced her to open it. In any case, he did not object to the photos at trial when they were formally offered, so his objection was waived. (2) He was guilty. The elements were proven: AAA was a child; he induced her to produce child pornography; and it was done through electronic means. The sweetheart defense does not apply to child pornography. The crime is mala in se (wrong in itself), so criminal intent must be proven, and his intent was shown. Since it was committed through a computer system, the penalty is one degree higher than under R.A. No. 9775.
cases.keyDoctrine: The Bill of Rights' exclusionary rule on privacy of communication (Art. III, Sec. 3(2) of the Constitution) applies only to evidence obtained by the State or its agents, not by private individuals. Privacy violations between private persons are governed by the Civil Code, the Data Privacy Act, and other laws, while admissibility is governed by the Rules on Evidence. A person who voluntarily gives someone else their account password limits their reasonable expectation of privacy as to that person. The Data Privacy Act allows processing of sensitive personal information when it relates to determining criminal liability or is needed to protect lawful rights in court proceedings.

cases.name: Regala v. Sandiganbayan
cases.subject: Mercantile Law
cases.facts: In 1987 the Republic, through the Presidential Commission on Good Government (PCGG), sued Eduardo Cojuangco, Jr. and others before the Sandiganbayan to recover alleged ill-gotten wealth, including shares in several corporations. Also sued were lawyers who were partners of the ACCRA Law Firm, including Teodoro Regala, Edgardo Angara, and Raul Roco, plus Paraja Hayudini, who had left the firm. As part of their legal services, ACCRA lawyers helped clients organize and acquire companies and, following office practice, acted as nominee-stockholders (holding shares in their own names for clients). They gave clients the stock certificates endorsed in blank and blank deeds of trust or assignment. The PCGG dropped Roco from the case because he supposedly promised to reveal the identity of the client for whom he acted as nominee. The other ACCRA lawyers asked for the same treatment. The PCGG said it would drop them only if they (a) disclosed the identity of their clients, (b) submitted documents showing the lawyer-client relationship, and (c) submitted the deeds of assignment they executed in favor of their clients. The lawyers refused, invoking the attorney-client privilege, and the Sandiganbayan denied their request to be excluded. (The petition of Hayudini, G.R. No. 108113, was decided together with this one.)
cases.issue: (1) Can the ACCRA lawyers refuse to reveal the identity of their clients on the ground of attorney-client privilege? (2) Did dropping Roco but not the other lawyers violate the equal protection clause?
cases.ruling: The Sandiganbayan resolutions were annulled, and it was ordered to exclude the petitioning lawyers from the case. (1) Yes, the lawyers may refuse. The lawyers were sued only to pressure them into naming their clients, so the PCGG could go after the 'bigger fish.' Their inclusion was based only on services they performed as lawyers, so the PCGG had no valid cause of action against them. The general rule is that a lawyer may not refuse to reveal a client's identity. The reasons: the court has a right to know the client is real, the privilege exists only once there is a client, the privilege covers the subject matter of the relationship, and an opposing party is entitled to know who their opponent is. But there are exceptions. Client identity is privileged: (a) where there is a strong probability that revealing the client's name would implicate the client in the very activity for which they sought the lawyer's advice; (b) where disclosure would open the client to civil liability; and (c) where the client's name would furnish the only link that would form the chain of testimony needed to convict the client of a crime. In short, a client's identity is privileged when the name itself has an independent significance, such that disclosing it would reveal client confidences. This case falls under at least two exceptions. The PCGG's conditions showed that the clients consulted the lawyers about the corporate set-up in question, so naming them would implicate them in the very activity for which they sought advice and would supply the missing link for the case against them. The Court distinguished between a client who hires a lawyer to plan an illegal act (not privileged) and a client who thinks they may have already done something illegal and asks a lawyer about it (privileged). The privilege also continues even after the lawyer-client relationship ends. (2) Yes, equal protection was violated. There was no proof that Roco actually revealed his client's identity, and he and the others were similarly situated. The PCGG's demand also violated the lawyers' right against self-incrimination and was a 'fishing expedition.'
cases.keyDoctrine: As a general rule, a lawyer may not refuse to reveal a client's identity. But the identity is privileged when the client's name has an independent significance, such that disclosing it would reveal client confidences. Examples: (1) a strong probability that revealing the name would implicate the client in the very activity for which legal advice was sought; (2) disclosure would open the client to civil liability; or (3) the name is the only link needed to form the chain of testimony to convict the client. The privilege does not protect a client who seeks advice in order to commit a future illegal act.

cases.name: Integrated Bar of the Philippines v. Purisima
cases.subject: Mercantile Law
cases.facts: In 2014, Finance Secretary Cesar Purisima, on the recommendation of BIR Commissioner Kim Jacinto-Henares, issued Revenue Regulations No. 4-2014 to monitor the service fees of self-employed professionals. It required them to: (a) submit an affidavit stating their rates, manner of billing, and the factors they consider in setting fees; (b) register their books of account and their official appointment books, which would contain only the clients' names and the date and time of each meeting; and (c) issue a BIR-registered receipt showing a 100% discount for pro bono (free) services. The Integrated Bar of the Philippines (IBP) and the Association of Small Accounting Practitioners in the Philippines challenged the regulation before the Supreme Court. The Philippine College of Physicians, Philippine Medical Association, and Philippine Dental Association joined. They argued that it violated their clients' and patients' right to privacy and their professions' rules on confidentiality, and that it went beyond what the Tax Code allows. The Office of the Solicitor General later sided with the petitioners on some points. The government argued that only names and appointment dates would be disclosed, which are not privileged.
cases.issue: Do the requirements of Revenue Regulations No. 4-2014, especially the mandatory registration of appointment books, violate the right to privacy of professionals and their clients and patients, and the confidentiality rules of their professions?
cases.ruling: The petitions were partly granted. (1) Registering books of account and issuing receipts for pro bono services are valid. (2) The affidavit of rates, billing, and fee factors is void because it goes beyond the Tax Code. It serves no legitimate purpose, although it does not encroach on the Court's rule-making power or violate ethical norms. (3) The mandatory registration of appointment books is void because it is an unconstitutional intrusion into the right to privacy. The Court explained that privacy covers 'zones of privacy' and three strands: locational, informational, and decisional privacy. Informational privacy is the right to control the processing (acquisition, disclosure, and use) of personal information. To decide whether a government intrusion is impermissible, the court asks whether the person showed a reasonable expectation of privacy and, if so, whether it was violated by unreasonable government intrusion. Clients and patients reasonably expect privacy when they set appointments with professionals. Examples: a battered wife who does not want it known she is seeing a lawyer, or a patient seeing a specialist. Names and dates alone 'paint no picture,' but as Disini v. Secretary of Justice teaches, gathered together they can reveal a pattern of behavior, and that pattern is protected. The mere chance that the State may look into this information is already an unreasonable intrusion. (4) The requirement also violates professional confidentiality. Citing Regala v. Sandiganbayan, a client's identity may be privileged in proper cases, so the government was wrong to say names are never privileged. The Data Privacy Act generally prohibits processing sensitive personal information and privileged information, which includes privileged communications under the Rules of Court, except in the cases listed in Section 13. Physician-patient communications are also privileged, and accountants' working papers are confidential under the Philippine Accountancy Act. The DOF and BIR were permanently stopped from implementing the void parts.
cases.keyDoctrine: Requiring self-employed professionals to register appointment books containing their clients' or patients' names and meeting times is an unconstitutional intrusion into the right to privacy. Clients and patients have a reasonable expectation of privacy in their consultations. Even if names and dates alone reveal little, put together they can show a protected pattern of behavior, and the mere chance that the State may look at them is an unreasonable intrusion. Under the Data Privacy Act, processing privileged information, including privileged communications under the Rules of Court, is generally prohibited except in the cases listed in Section 13.

cases.name: Garcia v. Executive Secretary
cases.subject: Mercantile Law
cases.facts: Congressman Enrique T. Garcia (Second District of Bataan) asked the Supreme Court to strike down Republic Act No. 7042, the Foreign Investments Act of 1991. He said it defeats the constitutional policy of building a self-reliant and independent national economy effectively controlled by Filipinos, and of protecting Filipino enterprises against unfair foreign competition. He pointed to these parts of the law: (1) Section 5 lets a foreign investor do business in the Philippines or invest in a domestic enterprise up to 100% of its capital without need of prior approval; the investor only has to register with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) or, for a single proprietorship, the Bureau of Trade Regulation and Consumer Protection (BTRCP). (2) Section 7 allows non-Philippine nationals to own up to 100% of domestic market enterprises unless foreign ownership is prohibited or limited by existing law or the Foreign Investment Negative List in Section 8. (3) The Negative List (Lists A, B and C) is not a true regulation, he argued, because List A only repeats what the Constitution and other laws already reserve to Filipinos. (4) Section 9 puts on a Filipino the burden of showing that an area should be included in List C. (5) The law repeals Articles 44 to 56 of the Omnibus Investments Code, and its transitory provisions allow practically unlimited foreign entry for three years. The Solicitor General answered that "without need of prior approval" applies only to equity restrictions. He said the law removed the case-to-case authorization of the Board of Investments, and that registration with the SEC or BTRCP is itself regulation of foreign investments. Senator Vicente T. Paterno intervened to defend the Act, and the Philippine Association of Battery Manufacturers intervened to support the petitioner.
cases.issue: Does RA 7042 violate the constitutional policy of a self-reliant and independent national economy effectively controlled by Filipinos, and the protection of Filipino enterprises against unfair foreign competition? And was the petition properly before the Court (an actual case, a proper party, raised at the right time)?
cases.ruling: The petition was dismissed. (1) The Court agreed that there was no actual case or controversy yet, mainly because the Act's implementing rules were still missing. A controversy must be "ripe" for determination, not conjectural or anticipatory. (2) Even so, Congressman Garcia, as a citizen, taxpayer and member of the House of Representatives, was a proper party, because he is someone who has sustained or is in danger of sustaining an injury from the act complained of. (3) The constitutional question was not raised too late; it was raised too early (prematurely). (4) On the merits, the challenge failed because the petitioner did not show an indubitable ground for it, or even a necessity to resolve it. Courts avoid ruling on constitutional questions and presume that acts of the political departments are valid unless there is a clear and unmistakable showing to the contrary ("To doubt is to sustain"). This rests on the separation of powers, and on the idea that a law, as the joint act of Congress and the President, was carefully studied and found consistent with the Constitution before it was enacted. (5) In light of the explanations of the Solicitor General and the intervenor, the petitioner had not proved unconstitutionality, and the Court was satisfied that the Act does not violate the constitutional provisions he mentioned. (6) What the petitioner raised was a debate on the wisdom or efficacy of the Act, which the Court is not competent to rule on. Debatable questions are for the legislature, and the Court may not annul an act of the political departments just because it is unwise or impractical. The Court found no grave abuse of discretion. The petitioner's objections were "expressed in the wrong forum"; Congress, which has the power to rewrite the law, is the place to hear them.
cases.keyDoctrine: A court will not strike down a law as unconstitutional unless there is an actual, **ripe** controversy and a clear and unmistakable showing that the law violates the Constitution: **"To doubt is to sustain."** Whether a law is wise, just or expedient is for the legislature to decide, not the courts.

cases.name: Gamboa v. Teves
cases.subject: Mercantile Law
cases.facts: Wilson P. Gamboa (later substituted by his heirs) asked the Supreme Court to compel the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) to look into whether the Philippine Long Distance Telephone Company (PLDT), a public utility, complied with the constitutional rule that only Filipinos, or corporations at least 60% of whose "capital" is owned by Filipinos, may operate a public utility (Section 11, Article XII of the 1987 Constitution). The petition was one for declaratory relief, which the Court treated as one for mandamus. In its 28 June 2011 Decision, the Court defined "capital" in that provision as shares with voting rights, as well as with full beneficial ownership, and directed the SEC to apply that definition to PLDT. This is the Court's 9 October 2012 Resolution on the motions for reconsideration of that Decision, filed by the Philippine Stock Exchange's President, Manuel V. Pangilinan, Napoleon L. Nazareno and the SEC. The movants argued, among other things, that: (1) the petition should have been dismissed as a procedurally defective petition for declaratory relief; (2) the Court changed a long-standing definition of "capital" (the total outstanding shares, voting or non-voting) that the SEC had always used; (3) PLDT was an indispensable party that was never heard; and (4) the ruling would drive away foreign investments. The undisputed facts on PLDT were that foreigners own 64.27% of its common shares (the only shares that vote for directors), Filipinos own 35.73% of the common shares, and the preferred shares (99.44% owned by Filipinos) have no voting rights. The Office of the Solicitor General agreed with the Court's definition of "capital".
cases.issue: Should the motions for reconsideration be granted? In particular: (1) was it proper to treat the petition for declaratory relief as one for mandamus; (2) did the Court change a long-standing rule or redefine "capital"; (3) what does "capital" in Section 11, Article XII of the Constitution mean, and does the 60-40 rule apply to each class of shares; (4) is PLDT an indispensable party; and (5) from when may sanctions be imposed?
cases.ruling: The motions for reconsideration were denied with finality. (1) The issue has far-reaching implications for the national economy, so treating the petition as one for mandamus was justified. (2) There was no change of any long-standing rule: for more than 75 years the Court had never interpreted or defined "capital" in the 1935, 1973 and 1987 Constitutions, and the SEC and DOJ opinions were conflicting. Opinions of SEC legal officers are not SEC rules (only the SEC en banc can issue opinions with the force of rules), and agency interpretations never bind the Court. (3) "Capital" in Section 11 refers to shares with voting rights, as well as with full beneficial ownership. Both the Voting Control Test and the Beneficial Ownership Test must be applied, and the 60-40 requirement applies separately to each class of shares (common, preferred non-voting, preferred voting or any other). The Foreign Investments Act of 1991 and its predecessor laws defined a "Philippine national" in the same way, and the framers of the Constitution intended Filipino control. (4) PLDT is an indispensable party only on the factual issues, which the Court left to the SEC; due process will be given to PLDT before the SEC. (5) The SEC may impose sanctions only if it finds, after due hearing, an existing violation at the start of its administrative case; public utilities can cure deficiencies before then. The Court stressed that it has no power to amend the Constitution, and that a different reading would let foreigners take effective control of the national economy, as under the Parity Amendment.
cases.keyDoctrine: "Capital" in Section 11, Article XII of the Constitution means **shares with voting rights and full beneficial ownership**. To own and operate a public utility, a corporation must have at least **60% Filipino ownership of each class of its shares**, so that Filipinos have effective control.

cases.name: GIOS-Samar, Inc. v. DOTC
cases.subject: Mercantile Law
cases.facts: In December 2014 the Department of Transportation and Communications (DOTC) and the Civil Aviation Authority of the Philippines (CAAP) invited bids for the development, operations and maintenance of six airports (Bacolod-Silay, Davao, Iloilo, Laguindingan, New Bohol (Panglao) and Puerto Princesa), worth P116.23 billion, through concession agreements with the private sector under the BOT Law (RA No. 6957, as amended by RA No. 7718). The concession period was 30 years. In March 2015 the DOTC and CAAP "bundled" five of the projects into two: Bundle 1 (Bacolod-Silay and Iloilo) and Bundle 2 (Davao, Laguindingan and New Bohol). GIOS-SAMAR, Inc., a non-governmental organization of subsistence farmers and fisherfolk from Samar, sued as a taxpayer, invoked "transcendental importance", and filed a petition for prohibition directly with the Supreme Court to stop the bidding. It argued that bundling: (1) violates the anti-dummy and public-utility provisions (Section 11, Article XII of the Constitution) and shuts out qualified Filipino companies; (2) creates a monopoly prohibited by Section 19, Article XII; (3) is an undue restraint of trade; (4) was done with grave abuse of discretion and without legal authority; and (5) makes a mockery of public bidding. The DOTC answered that the petition was premature and speculative, and the CAAP argued that the petition violated the doctrine of hierarchy of courts.
cases.issue: Is the bundling of the airport projects constitutional? And may the petitioner bring this petition directly to the Supreme Court, given the doctrine of hierarchy of courts, when its arguments depend on questions of fact?
cases.ruling: The petition was dismissed. (1) The petitioner's arguments are "inextricably intertwined with underlying questions of fact" that require the reception of evidence, and the Court is not a trier of fact. (2) Monopolies: the Constitution does not prohibit monopolies per se, and granting a concession to a winning bidder to develop, operate and maintain airports does not by itself create a monopoly that violates the Constitution, because exclusivity is inherent in a concession to deliver a public service. The Philippine Competition Act (RA No. 10667) does not penalize merely having a dominant position, but abusing it; showing that would take evidence on the relevant market, dominance and abusive conduct. The same is true of the claim that bundling is an anti-competitive agreement. (3) The anti-dummy and Section 11, Article XII claims failed because the petitioner did not allege facts showing that any corporation falsely simulated Filipino ownership, or that any law reserves such projects for Filipino-owned corporations (Executive Order No. 65 even exempts BOT infrastructure contracts from the 40% foreign ownership limit); the "shady companies" and "grave abuse of discretion" claims also raised factual questions or were bare conclusions of law. (4) Direct recourse to the Court is proper only for questions of law. The doctrine of hierarchy of courts is a constitutional filtering mechanism and a "bright-line rule" that cannot be set aside by invoking transcendental importance. The Court reviewed its history: the Angara model of direct recourse, the transcendental importance doctrine, the Diocese of Bacolod exceptions, and why hierarchy of courts is a constitutional imperative (the structure of the judicial system and due process). The only case in which the Court may take up factual questions at the first instance is the review of the factual basis of a martial law proclamation under Section 18, Article VII.
cases.keyDoctrine: The Supreme Court is **not a trier of facts**. Direct recourse to it is proper only for **pure questions of law**; when a factual issue is indispensable, the Court refuses to rule even if the case is said to be of **transcendental importance**, and the petition must first go to the proper trial court or the Court of Appeals. Granting an exclusive concession to a winning bidder is not by itself a prohibited monopoly.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Marites suspects her husband Ramon of having an affair. While Ramon is away, she goes to his law office, forces open his locked desk drawers, and takes private letters between Ramon and another woman, along with his diaries. She plans to present them as evidence in her petition for legal separation. Ramon objects, invoking his right to privacy. Marites argues that, as his wife, she cannot be barred from discovering proof of his infidelity. Are the letters and diaries admissible? Explain.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. Under Zulueta v. Court of Appeals, the letters and diaries are inadmissible.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: The Constitution declares the privacy of communication and correspondence inviolable. The only exception is a lawful order of the court, or when public safety or order requires otherwise, as prescribed by law. Evidence obtained in violation of this is inadmissible for any purpose in any proceeding. In Zulueta, the Court held that this applies even when the person who violated it is the spouse.
suggestedAnswer.application: Marites took Ramon's private correspondence and diaries by forcing open his drawers, without his knowledge or consent. There was no court order and no public safety or order reason. Being his wife does not change this. In Zulueta, the Court said the intimacies between husband and wife do not justify either one breaking the other's drawers and cabinets to look for evidence of infidelity, and a person does not give up their right to privacy by marrying.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The letters and diaries are inadmissible in the legal separation case. (Note: in Cadajas v. People, 2021, the Court later described this pronouncement in Zulueta as an obiter dictum, meaning a side remark that is not a binding precedent.)

keyPoints: Privacy of communication and correspondence is inviolable (1987 Constitution, Art. III, Sec. 3)
Only exceptions: lawful court order, or public safety or order as prescribed by law
Evidence obtained in violation is inadmissible for any purpose in any proceeding
The protection applies even against one's spouse; marriage does not waive privacy
Conclusion: the evidence is inadmissible

source.excerpt: The constitutional injunction declaring "the privacy of communication and correspondence [to be] inviolable" is no less applicable simply because it is the wife (who thinks herself aggrieved by her husband's infidelity) who is the party against whom the constitutional provision is to be enforced. Any violation of this provision renders the evidence obtained inadmissible "for any purpose in any proceeding." The intimacies between husband and wife do not justify any one of them in breaking the drawers and cabinets of the other and in ransacking them for any telltale evidence of marital infidelity. A person, by contracting marriage, does not shed his/her integrity or his right to privacy as an individual and the constitutional protection is ever available to him or to her.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Lito argues that the law guarantees "absolute freedom of communication between the spouses," so his wife has no right to keep her private papers from him, and he may use them as evidence against her. How did the Supreme Court in Zulueta v. Court of Appeals address the relationship between spousal privilege and the right to privacy?

suggestedAnswer.answer: The argument fails. The Court said the freedom of communication between spouses is different from forcing each spouse to share what they know with the other.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Zulueta, the Court explained that the law insures absolute freedom of communication between the spouses by making it privileged. Neither spouse may testify for or against the other without the other's consent while the marriage subsists. Neither may be examined, without the other's consent, about any communication received in confidence from the other during the marriage, save for specified exceptions.
suggestedAnswer.application: This privilege protects communications between the spouses from being disclosed. It does not give one spouse a right to take the other's private papers. The Court stressed that freedom of communication is one thing, but a compulsion for each one to share what one knows with the other is quite another. It added that this has nothing to do with the duty of fidelity each spouse owes the other.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Lito cannot rely on the spousal privilege to justify taking and using his wife's private papers. Each spouse keeps their constitutional right to privacy.

keyPoints: The law makes communication between spouses privileged to ensure freedom of communication
Spouses cannot testify for or against each other without consent while the marriage subsists (with exceptions)
Freedom of communication is different from forcing each spouse to share what they know
This has nothing to do with the duty of fidelity
Conclusion: spousal privilege does not allow one spouse to take the other's private papers

source.part: Ruling, last paragraph before the dispositive portion
source.excerpt: The law insures absolute freedom of communication between the spouses by making it privileged. Neither husband nor wife may testify for or against the other without the consent of the affected spouse while the marriage subsists. Neither may be examined without the consent of the other as to any communication received in confidence by one from the other during the marriage, save for specified exceptions. But one thing is freedom of communication; quite another is a compulsion for each one to share what one knows with the other. And this has nothing to do with the duty of fidelity that each owes to the other.

The disbarment ruling only meant he did not violate the injunction
It did not establish that the papers were admissible
Once the TRO was lifted, the ban on using the papers applied again

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Dr. Santos runs a small dental clinic on her lot. Only patients with appointments and her staff are allowed inside. Her neighbor, with whom she has a long-running boundary dispute, installs a rotating CCTV camera on his building that covers a large part of her clinic and lot. He says the camera is for security. Dr. Santos sues to have it removed, citing Article 26(1) of the Civil Code. The neighbor argues that Article 26(1) protects only the privacy of a 'residence,' and her property is a clinic. Decide.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Dr. Santos should win. Article 26(1) of the Civil Code is not limited to residences, and the camera violates her right to privacy.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Article 26(1) of the Civil Code makes 'prying into the privacy of another's residence' and similar acts a cause of action for damages, prevention and other relief. In Spouses Hing v. Choachuy, Sr., the Court held that this protection should not be confined to a house or residence. It may extend to places where a person has the right to exclude the public or deny them access, such as a business office where the public is excluded and only allowed persons may enter. Courts use the 'reasonable expectation of privacy' test.
suggestedAnswer.application: Dr. Santos's clinic is a place where she excludes the public and admits only patients and staff, so it falls within the protection. She has a reasonable expectation of privacy there. In Hing, the Court said cameras should not cover places where there is a reasonable expectation of privacy unless the affected person consents. Using them to pry into another's residence or business office would be no different from eavesdropping. The neighbor's camera covers a large part of her property without her consent.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The camera violates Dr. Santos's right to privacy. The court may order it removed or redirected away from her property.

keyPoints: Article 26(1) of the Civil Code: prying into the privacy of another's residence, and similar acts
The protection extends beyond residences to places where one may exclude the public, like a business office
Reasonable expectation of privacy test
Cameras may not cover places with a reasonable expectation of privacy without consent
Conclusion: the camera violates her privacy and may be ordered removed

source.part: Our Ruling, discussion of Article 26(1) of the Civil Code (including the Court's quotation of Arturo M. Tolentino), and of the RTC's finding that the Court upheld
source.excerpt: This does not mean, however, that only the residence is entitled to privacy, because the law covers also "similar acts." A business office is entitled to the same privacy when the public is excluded therefrom and only such individuals as are allowed to enter may come in. … Thus, an individual's right to privacy under Article 26(1) of the Civil Code should not be confined to his house or residence as it may extend to places where he has the right to exclude the public or deny them access. The phrase "prying into the privacy of another's residence," therefore, covers places, locations, or even situations which an individual considers as private. And as long as his right is recognized by society, other individuals may not infringe on his right to privacy. … The RTC, thus, considered that petitioners have a "reasonable expectation of privacy" in their property, whether they use it as a business office or as a residence and that the installation of video surveillance cameras directly facing petitioners' property or covering a significant portion thereof, without their consent, is a clear violation of their right to privacy. As we see then, the issuance of a preliminary injunction was justified.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: What is the 'reasonable expectation of privacy' test, as explained in Spouses Hing v. Choachuy, Sr.? How is it applied?

suggestedAnswer.answer: It is the test courts use to determine whether a person has a reasonable expectation of privacy and whether that expectation has been violated.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Hing, citing Ople v. Torres, the Court said the reasonableness of a person's expectation of privacy depends on a two-part test: (1) whether, by his conduct, the individual has exhibited an expectation of privacy; and (2) whether this expectation is one that society recognizes as reasonable.
suggestedAnswer.application: Customs, community norms, and practices may limit or extend a person's reasonable expectation of privacy. So the test is applied case by case, depending on the facts. In Hing, the Court agreed with the trial court that the spouses had a reasonable expectation of privacy in their property, whether used as a business office or a residence. Cameras facing their property or covering a significant part of it, without their consent, clearly violated their privacy.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The test has two parts, one subjective (did the person show an expectation of privacy) and one about society (is it reasonable), and it is decided case by case.

keyPoints: First part: by their conduct, the person exhibited an expectation of privacy
Second part: society recognizes the expectation as reasonable
Customs, community norms and practices may limit or extend it
Determined case by case, depending on the facts

source.part: Our Ruling, discussion of the reasonable expectation of privacy test
source.excerpt: In ascertaining whether there is a violation of the right to privacy, courts use the "reasonable expectation of privacy" test. This test determines whether a person has a reasonable expectation of privacy and whether the expectation has been violated. In Ople v. Torres, we enunciated that "the reasonableness of a person's expectation of privacy depends on a two-part test: (1) whether, by his conduct, the individual has exhibited an expectation of privacy; and (2) this expectation is one that society recognizes as reasonable." Customs, community norms, and practices may, therefore, limit or extend an individual's "reasonable expectation of privacy." Hence, the reasonableness of a person's expectation of privacy must be determined on a case-to-case basis since it depends on the factual circumstances surrounding the case.

questions.prompt: Spouses Reyes sue brothers Carlo and Paolo for installing surveillance cameras facing the Reyes property. The brothers answer that the cameras are on a building owned by their family corporation, not by them. They say they are mere stockholders and so are not the proper parties. The records show the corporation is family-owned and managed by the brothers' family, and the brothers let the court inspect the building and explained the camera set-up. Are the brothers proper parties? Explain, based on Spouses Hing v. Choachuy, Sr.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Yes, the brothers are proper parties to the suit.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Under Section 2, Rule 3 of the Rules of Court, a real party in interest is the party who stands to be benefited or injured by the judgment. A real party defendant is one who has a correlative legal obligation to redress a wrong done to the plaintiff by reason of the defendant's act or omission. In Hing, the Court held that not being the registered owners of the building does not automatically mean the defendants did not cause the cameras to be installed.
suggestedAnswer.application: As in Hing, the corporation is family-owned and managed by the defendants' family. The defendants acted as if they were the owners: they allowed the court inside for an inspection and explained the camera set-up. In Hing, the Court found that in such circumstances the personalities of the defendants and the corporation 'seem to merge,' and that the defendants were merely using the corporate fiction as a shield.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The brothers cannot hide behind the corporation's separate personality. They are proper parties to the suit.

keyPoints: A real party defendant has a correlative legal obligation to redress the wrong done to the plaintiff
Not owning the building does not automatically mean they did not cause the cameras to be installed
Family-owned corporation managed by their family; they acted as owners (allowed inspection)
The corporate fiction cannot be used as a shield
Conclusion: they are proper parties

source.part: Our Ruling, discussion of whether respondents are the proper parties
source.excerpt: In ruling that respondents are not the proper parties, the CA reasoned that since they do not own the building, they could not have installed the video surveillance cameras. Such reasoning, however, is erroneous. The fact that respondents are not the registered owners of the building does not automatically mean that they did not cause the installation of the video surveillance cameras. … He also admitted that as early as 1998 there has already been a dispute between his family and the Choachuy family concerning the boundaries of their respective properties. With these factual circumstances in mind, we believe that respondents are the proper parties to be impleaded. Moreover, although Aldo has a juridical personality separate and distinct from its stockholders, records show that it is a family-owned corporation managed by the Choachuy family. Also quite telling is the fact that respondents, notwithstanding their claim that they are not owners of the building, allowed the court to enter the compound of Aldo and conduct an ocular inspection. … Noticeably, in these instances, the personalities of respondents and Aldo seem to merge. All these taken together lead us to the inevitable conclusion that respondents are merely using the corporate fiction of Aldo as a shield to protect themselves from this suit.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Bea, a 16-year-old student, posts photos of herself at a party on Facebook. She claims the post was set so that only a few close friends could see it, but she offers no proof other than her own testimony. One of her Facebook friends, using his own account, shows the photos to a school official, who then disciplines Bea. Bea's parents file a petition for a writ of habeas data, claiming the school violated her right to informational privacy. Will the petition prosper? Explain.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. Under Vivares v. St. Theresa's College, the petition will not prosper because there was no proven violation of Bea's right to informational privacy.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: The writ of habeas data requires a showing, at least by substantial evidence, of an actual or threatened violation of the right to privacy in life, liberty or security. In Vivares, the Court held that before a user can have an expectation of privacy in social media activity, the user must show the intention to keep certain posts private by using measures to prevent or limit access, such as the platform's privacy tools.
suggestedAnswer.application: Bea's only proof that she limited the post is her own testimony. In Vivares, the Court gave little weight to similar self-serving statements without corroboration. Also, the photos were shown by a Facebook friend who had legitimate access to them, using his own account. In Vivares, the Court said the school officials were mere recipients who did not use unlawful means, since the information was voluntarily given to them by persons with legitimate access. Any fault would lie with the friend, not the school.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Without proof that Bea placed the photos within her protected zone of privacy, she cannot claim an expectation of privacy over them. The petition should be denied.

keyPoints: Habeas data needs substantial evidence of an actual or threatened violation of privacy in life, liberty or security
The user must show the intention to keep posts private by using privacy tools
Self-serving testimony without corroboration is not enough
The school officials were mere recipients from someone with legitimate access; no unlawful means were used
Conclusion: the petition is denied

source.part: Our Ruling, STC did not violate petitioners' daughters' right to privacy
source.excerpt: In sum, there can be no quibbling that the images in question, or to be more precise, the photos of minor students scantily clad, are personal in nature, likely to affect, if indiscriminately circulated, the reputation of the minors enrolled in a conservative institution. However, the records are bereft of any evidence, other than bare assertions that they utilized Facebook's privacy settings to make the photos visible only to them or to a select few. Without proof that they placed the photographs subject of this case within the ambit of their protected zone of privacy, they cannot now insist that they have an expectation of privacy with respect to the photographs in question.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A private school is sued in a petition for a writ of habeas data over students' photos it collected. The school argues that: (a) the writ applies only to extralegal killings and enforced disappearances; and (b) the writ applies only to entities in the business of gathering, collecting or storing data, which a school is not. Rule on both arguments, based on Vivares v. St. Theresa's College.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Both arguments are wrong.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Section 1 of the Rule on the Writ of Habeas Data makes it available against an unlawful act or omission of a public official or employee, or of a private individual or entity engaged in the gathering, collecting or storing of data or information about the aggrieved party. Section 2 allows any aggrieved party to file, and gives a separate list of who may file only for extralegal killings and enforced disappearances.
suggestedAnswer.application: (a) In Vivares, the Court said that if the writ were limited to extralegal killings and enforced disappearances, Section 2 would not have been worded that way. The Rule's annotations state that the writ can be availed of as an independent remedy to enforce the right to informational privacy. (b) To 'engage' in something means to do or take part in it. It does not require that the activity be done as a business. What matters is that the person or entity is gathering, collecting or storing data about the aggrieved party or their family.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The writ is not limited to extralegal killings and enforced disappearances, and it may be issued against a school even if the school is not in the business of collecting data. (In Vivares itself, the petition was still denied on the merits, because no privacy violation was proven.)

keyPoints: Section 2: 'any aggrieved party' may file, so the writ is not limited to extralegal killings and enforced disappearances
Habeas data is an independent remedy to enforce the right to informational privacy
'Engaged' means to do or take part in something, not necessarily as a business
What matters is that the respondent gathers, collects or stores data about the aggrieved party
Conclusion: both arguments fail

source.part: Our Ruling, procedural issues: the writ is not limited to extralegal killings and enforced disappearances (including the Court's quotation of the Rule's annotations), and the meaning of "engaged" in the gathering, collecting or storing of data
source.excerpt: Habeas data, to stress, was designed "to safeguard individual freedom from abuse in the information age." As such, it is erroneous to limit its applicability to extralegal killings and enforced disappearances only. … The writ of habeas data, however, can be availed of as an independent remedy to enforce one's right to privacy, more specifically the right to informational privacy. … Such individual or entity need not be in the business of collecting or storing data. To "engage" in something is different from undertaking a business endeavour. To "engage" means "to do or take part in something." It does not necessarily mean that the activity must be done in pursuit of a business. What matters is that the person or entity must be gathering, collecting or storing said data or information about the aggrieved party or his or her family.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A Facebook user argues that because her post was set to 'Friends' only, it was 'very private,' so anyone who is not her Facebook friend has no right to see it. Based on Vivares v. St. Theresa's College, is a 'Friends Only' post automatically private? What setting might have produced a different result?

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. A post set to 'Friends' cannot easily, much less automatically, be said to be very private.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Vivares, the Court held that a user who uses a privacy tool to grant or deny access should not be denied the informational privacy right that goes with that choice. But it also held that setting a post to 'Friends' is no assurance that it cannot be viewed by people who are not the user's Facebook friends.
suggestedAnswer.application: The Court gave these reasons: Facebook is designed to make the world more open and connected; many users 'befriend' total strangers; users often have hundreds of friends; and a friend can 'share' the post or 'tag' others who are not the user's friends, which expands the audience. The Court said that if access had been limited to the uploader through the 'Only Me' setting, or to a select few through the 'Custom' setting, the result may have been different, because the intention to limit access would be clearer.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: A 'Friends Only' post is not automatically private. Using 'Only Me' or a carefully chosen 'Custom' list more clearly shows an intention to keep a post private.

keyPoints: Using privacy tools is how a user claims informational privacy online
A 'Friends' setting is no assurance that non-friends cannot see the post
Friends can share or tag, which expands the audience; users often have hundreds of friends, including strangers
'Only Me' or 'Custom' settings may have changed the result
Conclusion: 'Friends Only' is not automatically private

source.part: Our Ruling, STC did not violate petitioners' daughters' right to privacy (the "Friends" setting, and the "Me Only" and "Custom" settings)
source.excerpt: It is well to emphasize at this point that setting a post's or profile detail's privacy to "Friends" is no assurance that it can no longer be viewed by another user who is not Facebook friends with the source of the content. The user's own Facebook friend can share said content or tag his or her own Facebook friend thereto, regardless of whether the user tagged by the latter is Facebook friends or not with the former. … Thus, it is suggested, that a profile, or even a post, with visibility set at "Friends Only" cannot easily, more so automatically, be said to be "very private," contrary to petitioners' argument. … Had it been proved that the access tothe pictures posted were limited to the original uploader, through the "Me Only" privacy setting, or that the user's contact list has been screened to limit access to a select few, through the "Custom" setting, the result may have been different, for in such instances, the intention to limit access to the particular post, instead of being broadcasted to the public at large or all the user's friends en masse, becomes more manifest and palpable.

C is wrong because no prior conviction is required. D is wrong because the Court said the writ will not issue merely on an alleged unauthorized access to information about a person.

The students showed the photos using their own accounts.

source.part: Our Ruling, STC did not violate petitioners' daughters' right to privacy

Respondents were mere recipients of what were posted. They did not resort to any unlawful means of gathering the information as it was voluntarily given to them by persons who had legitimate access to the said posts. Clearly, the fault, if any, lies with the friends of the minors.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Jessa, a private individual, takes screenshots of chat messages from Mark's messaging account without his knowledge, and gives them to the prosecutor. Mark is charged with a crime based on the messages. At trial, he moves to exclude them, arguing that under Article III, Section 3 of the Constitution, evidence obtained in violation of the privacy of communication is inadmissible. He also cites Zulueta v. Court of Appeals. Should the motion be granted? Explain, based on Cadajas v. People.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. The constitutional exclusionary rule does not apply, because the evidence was obtained by a private individual and not by the State.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Cadajas v. People, the Court held that the Bill of Rights is meant to protect private individuals against government intrusion, so its provisions do not apply between private individuals. The rule on admissibility under Article III must affect only evidence obtained by the State through its agents. The Court called the statement in Zulueta v. Court of Appeals a mere obiter dictum, not a binding precedent. Privacy violations between private individuals are governed by the Civil Code, the Data Privacy Act, and other laws. Admissibility is governed by the Rules on Evidence: relevance, materiality, authentication, and the exclusionary rules.
suggestedAnswer.application: Jessa is a private individual, not a police officer or other agent of the State. So Mark cannot invoke Article III, Section 3 to exclude the screenshots. His reliance on Zulueta fails because Cadajas explained that the pronouncement there was obiter: that petition was about the return of the documents, and the documents were excluded because of the trial court's injunction. Mark's remedy for any privacy violation by Jessa lies under the Civil Code, the Data Privacy Act, or other laws. The screenshots' admissibility will depend on the Rules on Evidence, such as proper authentication.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The motion should be denied on the constitutional ground. The evidence's admissibility is decided under the Rules on Evidence.

keyPoints: The Bill of Rights protects against the State, not against private individuals
The Article III exclusionary rule covers only evidence obtained by the State or its agents
Zulueta's statement on inadmissibility between spouses is obiter dictum
Privacy violations between private persons: Civil Code, Data Privacy Act, other laws
Admissibility: Rules on Evidence (relevance, materiality, authentication, exclusionary rules)

source.part: Our Ruling, on petitioner's right to privacy (the Bill of Rights as protection against the State, and Zulueta as obiter dictum)
source.excerpt: That the Bill of Rights embodied in the Constitution is not meant to be invoked against acts of private individuals finds support in the deliberations of the Constitutional Commission. … While the case of Zulueta v. Court of Appeals (Zulueta) may appear to carve out an exception to the abovementioned rule by recognizing the rule on inadmissibility of evidence between spouses when one obtains evidence in violation of his/her spouse's right to privacy, such a pronouncement is a mere obiter dictum that cannot be considered as a binding precedent. … At any rate, violation of the right to privacy between individuals is properly governed by the provisions of the Civil Code, the Data Privacy Act (DPA), and other pertinent laws, while its admissibility shall be governed by the rules on relevance, materiality, authentication of documents, and the exclusionary rules under the Rules on Evidence. In this case, the photographs and conversations in the Facebook Messenger account that were obtained and used as evidence against petitioner, which he considers as fruit of the poisonous tree, were not obtained through the efforts of the police officers or any agent of the State. Rather, these were obtained by a private individual. Indeed, the rule governing the admissibility of an evidence under Article III of the Constitution must affect only those pieces of evidence obtained by the State through its agents. It is these individuals who can flex government muscles and use government resources for a possible abuse. However, where private individuals are involved, for which their relationship is governed by the New Civil Code, the admissibility of an evidence cannot be determined by the provisions of the Bill of Rights.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Paolo gave his girlfriend the password to his messaging account. Later, she logs in and copies some of his messages, which are used as evidence against him. Paolo says his account is password-protected, so he had a reasonable expectation that no one else could access it, and his right to privacy was violated. Is he correct? Explain, applying Cadajas v. People.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. By voluntarily giving his password to his girlfriend, Paolo limited his reasonable expectation of privacy as to her, so there was no violation.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Cadajas, the Court applied the reasonable expectation of privacy test from Spouses Hing v. Choachuy, Sr. It held that a person who voluntarily gives his password to another, in effect, authorizes that person to access the account. This limits his reasonable expectation of privacy as to that person.
suggestedAnswer.application: Paolo's expectation of privacy came from his account being password-protected. But he does not claim it was hacked or accessed by unauthorized means. He gave his girlfriend the password and took no steps to exclude her. As in Cadajas, his expectation of privacy as to her was limited. The Court also said that once he made the contents available to her, she had the latitude to show others what she could access. In Cadajas, this was true even though the girl was forced by her mother to open the account.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: There was no violation of Paolo's right to privacy.

keyPoints: Reasonable expectation of privacy test (from Hing v. Choachuy)
A password-protected account gives an expectation of privacy
Voluntarily giving the password authorizes the other person's access
No hacking or unauthorized means were used
Conclusion: his expectation of privacy as to that person was limited; no violation

source.part: Our Ruling, on petitioner's right to privacy (application of the reasonable expectation of privacy test)
source.excerpt: Here, petitioner's expectation of privacy emanates from the fact that his Facebook Messenger account is password protected, such that no one can access the same except himself. Petitioner never asserted that his Facebook Messenger account was hacked or the photos were taken from his account through unauthorized means. Rather, the photos were obtained from his account because AAA, to whom he gave his password, had access to it. Considering that he voluntarily gave his password to AAA, he, in effect, has authorized AAA to access the same. He did not even take steps to exclude AAA from gaining access to his account. Having been given authority to access his Facebook Messenger account, petitioner's reasonable expectation of privacy, in so far as AAA is concerned, had been limited. Thus, there is no violation of privacy to speak of.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: During trial, the prosecution formally offers photos taken from the accused's online account. The accused's lawyer makes no objection. After conviction, the accused argues for the first time on appeal that the photos were inadmissible because they violated his right to privacy. Can the appellate court consider the objection? Explain, based on Cadajas v. People.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. The objection was waived because it was not made when the evidence was formally offered at trial.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Cadajas, the Court said that to exclude evidence, the objection must be made at the proper time and the grounds must be specified. For documentary evidence, the objection must be made when it is formally offered. A party who fails to object on time is considered to have waived the objection, even if the evidence would have been rejected had it been challenged properly. Also, no question will be considered on appeal unless it was raised in the proceedings below.
suggestedAnswer.application: The accused did not object when the photos were formally offered. Raising the issue for the first time on appeal is barred. In Cadajas, the accused was likewise deemed to have waived his objection, and the photos taken from his Facebook Messenger account were admissible.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The objection is waived, and the photos remain admissible.

keyPoints: An objection to evidence must be made at the proper time, with the grounds specified
For documentary evidence: object when it is formally offered
Failure to object on time means waiver, even if the evidence was inadmissible by nature
Issues cannot be raised for the first time on appeal
Conclusion: the objection is waived

source.part: Our Ruling, on petitioner's right to privacy (failure to object at trial, and issues raised for the first time on appeal)
source.excerpt: Basic is the rule that in order to exclude evidence, the objection to admissibility of evidence must be made at the proper time, and the grounds therefore be specified. Objection to evidence must be made at the time it is formally offered. … When a party failed to interpose a timely objection to evidence at the time they were offered in evidence, such objection shall be considered as waived. This is true even if by its nature the evidence is inadmissible and would have surely been rejected if it had been challenged at the proper time. As a complimentary principle, it is well-settled that no question will be entertained on appeal unless it has been raised in the proceedings below.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: In Cadajas v. People, how did the Court treat the statement in Zulueta v. Court of Appeals that evidence obtained by one spouse in violation of the other's privacy is inadmissible?

choices.A: As a binding precedent that applies to all private individuals
choices.B: As a mere obiter dictum that cannot be considered a binding precedent
choices.C: As overturned because it conflicts with the Data Privacy Act
choices.D: As applicable only to married couples

questions.explanation: B is correct. The Court said the pronouncement in Zulueta is a mere obiter dictum that cannot be considered a binding precedent. One reason is that the Zulueta petition only asked for the return of the documents. Another is that the documents were declared inadmissible because of the trial court's injunction, not because of Article III, Section 3. A is wrong because the Court said it is not binding. C is wrong because the Court did not base its treatment on any conflict with the Data Privacy Act. D is wrong because the Court did not keep it as a rule for spouses; it said the statement is not a binding precedent at all.

source.part: Our Ruling, on petitioner's right to privacy (discussion of Zulueta v. Court of Appeals)
source.excerpt: While the case of Zulueta v. Court of Appeals (Zulueta) may appear to carve out an exception to the abovementioned rule by recognizing the rule on inadmissibility of evidence between spouses when one obtains evidence in violation of his/her spouse's right to privacy, such a pronouncement is a mere obiter dictum that cannot be considered as a binding precedent. This is because the petition brought to the Court in Zulueta simply asked for the return of the documents seized by the wife and thus, pertained to the ownership of the documents therein. Moreover, documents were declared inadmissible because of the injunction order issued by the trial court and not on account of Art. III, Sec. 3 of the Constitution.

It also allows it when necessary to protect lawful rights and interests in court proceedings, as in Cadajas, where the evidence was used to establish AAA's claims. A is wrong because there is no blanket permission for any reason. C is wrong because being a minor is not a ground for processing; minors' data deserves more protection, not less. D is wrong because the decision does not say social media posts may be processed freely.

source.excerpt: As further pointed out by Associate Justice Rodil V. Zalameda during the deliberations of this case, the DPA allows the processing of data and sensitive personal information where it relates to the determination of criminal liability of a data subject, such as a violation of R.A. No. 10175 in relation to R.A. No. 9775 and when necessary for the protection of lawful rights and interests of persons in court proceedings, as in this case where the communications and photos sought to be excluded were submitted in evidence to establish AAA's legal claims before the prosecutor's office and the courts.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: In Cadajas v. People, the Court quoted Justice Leonen's separate concurring opinion on the aspects of the right to informational privacy. Which of the following is NOT one of the three aspects listed there?

choices.A: To keep inalienable information to themselves
choices.B: To prevent first disclosure
choices.C: To prevent further dissemination in case the information has already been disclosed
choices.D: To demand payment for any use of one's personal information

The three listed are: (1) to keep inalienable information to themselves; (2) to prevent first disclosure; and (3) to prevent further dissemination if the information has already been disclosed. The opinion added a possible fourth from the European Union, the right to be forgotten, but not a right to demand payment. A, B, and C are wrong answers because each is one of the three aspects.

source.excerpt: Thus, it has the following aspects: (1) to keep inalienable information to themselves; (2) to prevent first disclosure; and (3) to prevent further dissemination in case the information has already been disclosed.

questions.prompt: In Cadajas v. People, which of the following is NOT one of the facts the Court said must be proven to convict for child pornography (R.A. No. 9775, in relation to R.A. No. 10175)?

choices.B: The victim was induced or coerced to perform in the creation or production of any form of child pornography.
choices.C: The child pornography was performed through visual, audio or written combination thereof by electronic, mechanical, digital, optical, magnetic or any other means.

The Court also explained that the law punishes even mere possession, separately from possession with intent to sell or distribute. A, B, and C are wrong answers because they are exactly the three facts the Court said must be proven.
