questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A telephone company holds a franchise to operate a public utility. It has two classes of shares: common shares, which alone can vote in the election of directors, and preferred shares, which cannot. Foreigners own 60% of the common shares, while Filipinos own almost all the preferred shares, so that Filipinos hold more than 60% of all the shares combined. The company says it complies with the 60-40 ownership rule for public utilities because Filipinos own over 60% of its total shares. Based on the Resolution in Gamboa v. Teves, is the company correct?

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. The company does not meet the constitutional requirement, because "capital" in Section 11, Article XII refers to shares with voting rights as well as full beneficial ownership, and the 60-40 rule applies to each class of shares, not just to the total of all shares.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Under Section 11, Article XII of the 1987 Constitution, a public utility may be operated only by Filipino citizens or by corporations at least 60% of whose "capital" is owned by Filipinos. The Court held that mere legal title is insufficient: full beneficial ownership of 60% of the outstanding capital stock, coupled with 60% of the voting rights, is required. Both the Voting Control Test and the Beneficial Ownership Test must be applied. The requirement applies uniformly to all classes of shares. If a corporation issues common and preferred non-voting shares, at least 60% of the common shares and at least 60% of the preferred non-voting shares must be owned by Filipinos. The Foreign Investments Act defines a "Philippine national" corporation as one at least 60% of whose capital stock outstanding and entitled to vote is owned by Filipinos.
suggestedAnswer.application: Here, foreigners own 60% of the common shares, the only shares that vote for directors, so they control the election of the board and Filipinos do not have voting control. It does not help that Filipinos own most of the preferred shares: the 60-40 rule must be met separately in each class, and adding up all the shares would let foreigners keep effective control.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The company fails the 60-40 requirement, so it may not operate the public utility.

keyPoints: "Capital" in Section 11 means shares with voting rights and full beneficial ownership
Mere legal title is not enough
Both the Voting Control Test and the Beneficial Ownership Test must be applied
The 60-40 rule applies separately to each class of shares (common, preferred, etc.)
A Philippine national corporation has at least 60% of its capital stock entitled to vote owned by Filipinos
Foreigners holding 60% of the voting common shares means Filipinos lack effective control

source.part: Resolution, Part V (right to elect directors, coupled with beneficial ownership, translates to effective control)
source.excerpt: Both the Voting Control Test and the Beneficial Ownership Test must be applied to determine whether a corporation is a "Philippine national." … Since the constitutional requirement of at least 60 percent Filipino ownership applies not only to voting control of the corporation but also to the beneficial ownership of the corporation, it is therefore imperative that such requirement apply uniformly and across the board to all classes of shares, regardless of nomenclature and category, comprising the capital of a corporation. Under the Corporation Code, capital stock consists of all classes of shares issued to stockholders, that is, common shares as well as preferred shares, which may have different rights, privileges or restrictions as stated in the articles of incorporation. … Since a specific class of shares may have rights and privileges or restrictions different from the rest of the shares in a corporation, the 60-40 ownership requirement in favor of Filipino citizens in Section 11, Article XII of the Constitution must apply not only to shares with voting rights but also to shares without voting rights. Preferred shares, denied the right to vote in the election of directors, are anyway still entitled to vote on the eight specific corporate matters mentioned above. Thus, if a corporation, engaged in a partially nationalized industry, issues a mixture of common and preferred non-voting shares, at least 60 percent of the common shares and at least 60 percent of the preferred non-voting shares must be owned by Filipinos. Of course, if a corporation issues only a single class of shares, at least 60 percent of such shares must necessarily be owned by Filipinos. In short, the 60-40 ownership requirement in favor of Filipino citizens must apply separately to each class of shares, whether common, preferred non-voting, preferred voting or any other class of shares. This uniform application of the 60-40 ownership requirement in favor of Filipino citizens clearly breathes life to the constitutional command that the ownership and operation of public utilities shall be reserved exclusively to corporations at least 60 percent of whose capital is Filipino-owned. Applying uniformly the 60-40 ownership requirement in favor of Filipino citizens to each class of shares, regardless of differences in voting rights, privileges and restrictions, guarantees effective Filipino control of public utilities, as mandated by the Constitution.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Companies that relied on opinions of the SEC's legal officers and of the Department of Justice, which counted both voting and non-voting shares when measuring foreign ownership, argue that the Court changed a long-standing definition of "capital" midstream. Are they correct? Do those opinions bind the Court? Answer based on the Resolution in Gamboa v. Teves.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. The Court did not change any long-standing rule or redefine "capital", and the SEC and DOJ opinions do not bind the Court.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: For more than 75 years since the 1935 Constitution, the Court had never interpreted or defined the term "capital" in the 1935, 1973 and 1987 Constitutions, so there was no judicial precedent to overturn. The SEC and DOJ opinions on the meaning of "capital" were conflicting and inconsistent. Opinions of individual Commissioners or SEC legal officers are not SEC rules or regulations: under Sections 4.6 and 5.1(g) of the Securities Regulation Code, only the SEC en banc can issue opinions that have the force and effect of rules, and it cannot delegate the power to adopt rules. Even the opinions of the SEC en banc and the DOJ are neither conclusive nor controlling on the Court, because an agency's interpretation of the law is only preliminary, and the power to make the final interpretation of the law lies with the Court.
suggestedAnswer.application: The movants' claim that the 28 June 2011 Decision introduced a "new" definition is, in the Court's words, "patently wrong and utterly baseless", because there was never a Court ruling defining "capital" before. The SEC and DOJ had not consistently used the movants' definition: a 1985 DOJ opinion, for example, found a structure like PLDT's unconstitutional, and the SEC en banc itself adopted the Grandfather Rule. In any case, the opinions of SEC legal officers have no force of a rule, and the Court decides the final meaning of the constitutional term.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: There was no midstream redefinition, and the agency opinions cannot control the Court's interpretation of "capital".

keyPoints: No court had ever defined "capital" in the 1935, 1973 and 1987 Constitutions
SEC and DOJ opinions were conflicting and inconsistent
Opinions of SEC legal officers are not SEC rules or regulations
Only the SEC en banc can issue opinions with the force of rules, and it cannot delegate rule-making
Agency interpretations are only preliminary and never conclusive on the Court
The final interpretation of the Constitution lies with the Court

source.part: Resolution, Part II (no change of any long-standing rule) and the discussion of the SEC and DOJ opinions
source.excerpt: For more than 75 years since the 1935 Constitution, the Court has not interpreted or defined the term "capital" found in various economic provisions of the 1935, 1973 and 1987 Constitutions. There has never been a judicial precedent interpreting the term "capital" in the 1935, 1973 and 1987 Constitutions, until now. Hence, it is patently wrong and utterly baseless to claim that the Court in defining the term "capital" in its 28 June 2011 Decision modified, reversed, or set aside the purported long-standing definition of the term "capital," which supposedly refers to the total outstanding shares of stock, whether voting or non-voting. To repeat, until the present case there has never been a Court ruling categorically defining the term "capital" found in the various economic provisions of the 1935, 1973 and 1987 Philippine Constitutions. … The opinions of the SEC, as well as of the Department of Justice (DOJ), on the definition of the term "capital" as referring to both voting and non-voting shares (combined total of common and preferred shares) are, in the first place, conflicting and inconsistent. There is no basis whatsoever to the claim that the SEC and the DOJ have consistently and uniformly adopted a definition of the term "capital" contrary to the definition that this Court adopted in its 28 June 2011 Decision. … Thus, the act of the individual Commissioners or legal officers of the SEC in issuing opinions that have the effect of SEC rules or regulations is ultra vires. Under Sections 4.6 and 5.1(g) of the Code, only the SEC en banc can "issue opinions" that have the force and effect of rules or regulations. Section 4.6 of the Code bars the SEC en banc from delegating to any individual Commissioner or staff the power to adopt rules or regulations. In short, any opinion of individual Commissioners or SEC legal officers does not constitute a rule or regulation of the SEC. … Likewise, the opinions of the SEC en banc, as well as of the DOJ, interpreting the law are neither conclusive nor controlling and thus, do not bind the Court. It is hornbook doctrine that any interpretation of the law that administrative or quasi-judicial agencies make is only preliminary, never conclusive on the Court. The power to make a final interpretation of the law, in this case the term "capital" in Section 11, Article XII of the 1987 Constitution, lies with this Court, not with any other government entity.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A citizen asks the Court to define a term in the Constitution and to compel the SEC to investigate whether a public utility corporation complies with the nationality requirement. The Court defines the term and directs the SEC to apply the definition. The corporation complains that it was not made a party and that its property was taken without due process. The SEC also asks from when sanctions may be imposed. Based on the Resolution in Gamboa v. Teves, how should these be answered?

suggestedAnswer.answer: The Court limited itself to the purely legal question of what the constitutional term means. It did not decide whether the corporation violated the Constitution, so the corporation was not deprived of due process; due process is given before the SEC. Sanctions may be imposed only if the SEC finds, after due hearing, an existing violation at the start of its administrative case.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: A question that requires presenting and determining evidence at a hearing is generally outside the Court's jurisdiction but within the SEC's statutory powers. The corporation is an indispensable party only for the factual issues (for example, whether the foreign share of its common shares exceeds the 40% limit), which are for the SEC to decide. The Court's directive is addressed solely to the SEC, the agency that enforces the 60-40 rule. Under prevailing jurisprudence, public utilities that fail the nationality requirement can cure their deficiencies before the start of the administrative case or investigation.
suggestedAnswer.application: In Gamboa, the Court refrained from ruling on whether PLDT violated the 60-40 requirement and confined itself to the legal issue of defining "capital", leaving the factual questions to the SEC. PLDT therefore had no property taken and no denial of due process, because it can present proof to the SEC that it complies. The SEC may impose statutory sanctions only if, after due hearing, it finds a violation existing when its administrative case begins; a utility that cures its deficiency before then avoids sanctions.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: No denial of due process; factual questions go to the SEC with PLDT heard; sanctions only for a violation still existing at the start of the SEC's case.

keyPoints: The Court decided only the purely legal issue (the meaning of "capital")
Whether PLDT violated the rule is a factual question for the SEC after a hearing
The directive is addressed solely to the SEC, not to PLDT
Due process is given to PLDT when it presents proof to the SEC
Sanctions only if the SEC finds, after due hearing, an existing violation at the start of the case
Deficiencies can be cured before the start of the administrative case

source.part: Resolution, Parts VIII, IX and XI (the undisputed facts; PLDT not an indispensable party; prospective application of sanctions)
source.excerpt: Despite the foregoing facts, the Court did not decide, and in fact refrained from ruling on the question of whether PLDT violated the 60-40 ownership requirement in favor of Filipino citizens in Section 11, Article XII of the 1987 Constitution. Such question indisputably calls for a presentation and determination of evidence through a hearing, which is generally outside the province of the Court’s jurisdiction, but well within the SEC’s statutory powers. Thus, for obvious reasons, the Court limited its decision on the purely legal and threshold issue on the definition of the term "capital" in Section 11, Article XII of the Constitution and directed the SEC to apply such definition in determining the exact percentage of foreign ownership in PLDT. … Since the Court limited its resolution on the purely legal issue on the definition of the term "capital" in Section 11, Article XII of the 1987 Constitution, and directed the SEC to investigate any violation by PLDT of the 60-40 ownership requirement in favor of Filipino citizens under the Constitution, there is no deprivation of PLDT’s property or denial of PLDT’s right to due process, contrary to Pangilinan and Nazareno’s misimpression. Due process will be afforded to PLDT when it presents proof to the SEC that it complies, as it claims here, with Section 11, Article XII of the Constitution. … As discussed, the Court has directed the SEC to investigate and determine whether PLDT violated Section 11, Article XII of the Constitution. Thus, there is no dispute that it is only after the SEC has determined PLDT’s violation, if any exists at the time of the commencement of the administrative case or investigation, that the SEC may impose the statutory sanctions against PLDT. In other words, once the 28 June 2011 Decision becomes final, the SEC shall impose the appropriate sanctions only if it finds after due hearing that, at the start of the administrative case or investigation, there is an existing violation of Section 11, Article XII of the Constitution. Under prevailing jurisprudence, public utilities that fail to comply with the nationality requirement under Section 11, Article XII and the FIA can cure their deficiencies prior to the start of the administrative case or investigation.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: In Gamboa v. Teves, the Court treated a petition for declaratory relief as one for mandamus. What was its reason?

choices.A: The far-reaching implications of the issue on the national economy justified it
choices.B: The petition had no procedural defect at all
choices.C: The SEC asked the Court to treat it as mandamus
choices.D: The petition was filed by the Solicitor General

questions.explanation: A is correct. The Court said the interpretation of "capital" in Section 11, Article XII has far-reaching implications for the national economy, so "the far-reaching implications of this issue justify the treatment of the petition as one for mandamus." B is wrong because the Court acknowledged a "supposed procedural defect" in the petition and resolved the case anyway, as in Luzon Stevedoring. C is wrong because the Court gave its own reason, in the interest of substantial justice. D is wrong because the petitioner was Gamboa (later his heirs), not the Solicitor General.

source.part: Resolution, Part I (far-reaching implications justify treating the petition as one for mandamus)
source.excerpt: As we emphatically stated in the 28 June 2011 Decision, the interpretation of the term "capital" in Section 11, Article XII of the Constitution has far-reaching implications to the national economy. In fact, a resolution of this issue will determine whether Filipinos are masters, or second-class citizens, in their own country. What is at stake here is whether Filipinos or foreigners will have effective control of the Philippine national economy. Indeed, if ever there is a legal issue that has far-reaching implications to the entire nation, and to future generations of Filipinos, it is the threshold legal issue presented in this case. … Contrary to Pangilinan’s narrow view, the serious economic consequences resulting in the interpretation of the term "capital" in Section 11, Article XII of the Constitution undoubtedly demand an immediate adjudication of this issue. Simply put, the far-reaching implications of this issue justify the treatment of the petition as one for mandamus. … The circumstances surrounding the present case, such as the supposed procedural defect of the petition and the pivotal legal issue involved, resemble those in Luzon Stevedoring. Consequently, in the interest of substantial justice and faithful adherence to the Constitution, we opted to resolve this case for the guidance of the public and all concerned parties.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: According to the Resolution in Gamboa v. Teves, who can issue SEC opinions that have the force and effect of SEC rules and regulations?

choices.A: Any SEC legal officer
choices.B: Any individual Commissioner
choices.C: The SEC en banc only
choices.D: The SEC General Counsel, if the SEC en banc delegates the power

questions.explanation: C is correct. The Court said that only the SEC en banc can "issue opinions" that have the force and effect of rules or regulations, under Sections 4.6 and 5.1(g) of the Securities Regulation Code. A and B are wrong because any opinion of an individual Commissioner or SEC legal officer does not constitute a rule or regulation of the SEC; acts of such officers in issuing opinions that have the effect of rules are ultra vires. D is wrong because Section 4.6 bars the SEC en banc from delegating to any individual Commissioner or staff the power to adopt rules or regulations.

source.part: Resolution, Part II (the SEC opinions)
source.excerpt: The opinions issued by SEC legal officers do not have the force and effect of SEC rules and regulations because only the SEC en banc can adopt rules and regulations. As expressly provided in Section 4.6 of the Securities Regulation Code, the SEC cannot delegate to any of its individual Commissioner or staff the power to adopt any rule or regulation. Further, under Section 5.1 of the same Code, it is the SEC as a collegial body, and not any of its legal officers, that is empowered to issue opinions and approve rules and regulations. Thus: … Thus, the act of the individual Commissioners or legal officers of the SEC in issuing opinions that have the effect of SEC rules or regulations is ultra vires. Under Sections 4.6 and 5.1(g) of the Code, only the SEC en banc can "issue opinions" that have the force and effect of rules or regulations. Section 4.6 of the Code bars the SEC en banc from delegating to any individual Commissioner or staff the power to adopt rules or regulations. In short, any opinion of individual Commissioners or SEC legal officers does not constitute a rule or regulation of the SEC.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Under the Foreign Investments Act of 1991, as discussed in Gamboa v. Teves, a domestic corporation is a "Philippine national" only if:

choices.A: At least 60% of its capital stock outstanding and entitled to vote is owned by Filipino citizens
choices.B: At least 60% of its total assets are owned by Filipino citizens
choices.C: A majority of its authorized capital stock is held by Filipino citizens, whether voting or non-voting
choices.D: All its executive officers are Filipino citizens, whatever its ownership

questions.explanation: A is correct. The Court said the FIA defines a "Philippine national" as a Philippine citizen, or a domestic corporation at least "60% of the capital stock outstanding and entitled to vote" is owned by Philippine citizens; a domestic corporation is a Philippine national "only if at least 60% of its voting stock is owned by Filipino citizens." B is wrong because the test is about capital stock entitled to vote, not total assets. C is wrong because it counts non-voting shares and only a bare majority. D is wrong because officers' citizenship is not the test for being a Philippine national.

source.part: Resolution, Part IV (definition of "Philippine national")
source.excerpt: Thus, the FIA clearly and unequivocally defines a "Philippine national" as a Philippine citizen, or a domestic corporation at least "60% of the capital stock outstanding and entitled to vote" is owned by Philippine citizens. … The FIA, like all its predecessor statutes, clearly defines a "Philippine national" as a Filipino citizen, or a domestic corporation "at least sixty percent (60%) of the capital stock outstanding and entitled to vote" is owned by Filipino citizens. A domestic corporation is a "Philippine national" only if at least 60% of its voting stock is owned by Filipino citizens. This definition of a "Philippine national" is crucial in the present case because the FIA reiterates and clarifies Section 11, Article XII of the 1987 Constitution, which limits the ownership and operation of public utilities to Filipino citizens or to corporations or associations at least 60% Filipino-owned.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the last sentence of Section 11, Article XII of the 1987 Constitution, as quoted in Gamboa v. Teves?

choices.A: Foreign investors may take any seat on the board of a public utility if they own 40% of its capital
choices.B: Foreign investors' participation in the governing body is limited to their proportionate share in the capital, and all executive and managing officers must be Filipino citizens
choices.C: All directors and stockholders of a public utility must be Filipino citizens
choices.D: Foreign investors may serve as executive officers so long as Filipinos hold the majority of the board

questions.explanation: B is correct. The sentence reads: "The participation of foreign investors in the governing body of any public utility enterprise shall be limited to their proportionate share in its capital, and all the executive and managing officers of such corporation or association must be citizens of the Philippines." A is wrong because board participation is limited to the foreign investors' proportionate share in capital, not any seat. C is wrong because the Constitution does not bar foreign stockholders or directors altogether; it limits them proportionately. D is wrong because all executive and managing officers must be Filipino citizens.

source.part: Resolution, Part VII (last sentence of Section 11, Article XII)
source.excerpt: The last sentence of Section 11, Article XII of the 1987 Constitution reads: The participation of foreign investors in the governing body of any public utility enterprise shall be limited to their proportionate share in its capital, and all the executive and managing officers of such corporation or association must be citizens of the Philippines.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: In the Final Word of Gamboa v. Teves, how did the Court compare the movants' interpretation of "capital" with the Parity Amendment?

choices.A: It would bring back the same evils of the Parity Amendment, giving foreigners parity rights with Filipinos even without any constitutional amendment
choices.B: It would be a welcome improvement over the Parity Amendment
choices.C: It is unrelated to the Parity Amendment, which concerned only mining
choices.D: It would be valid because the Court can amend the Constitution if the economy requires it

questions.explanation: A is correct. The Court said the movants' interpretation "would bring us back to the same evils spawned by the Parity Amendment, effectively giving foreigners parity rights with Filipinos, but this time even without any amendment to the present Constitution." B and C are wrong because the Court treated the comparison as a warning, and the Parity Amendment covered natural resources and public utilities. D is wrong because the Court said any deviation from the 60% Filipino requirement needs an amendment of the Constitution, and the Court "has no power to amend the Constitution for its power and duty is only to faithfully apply and interpret the Constitution."

source.part: Resolution, Part XII (Final Word)
source.excerpt: Movants’ interpretation of the term "capital" would bring us back to the same evils spawned by the Parity Amendment, effectively giving foreigners parity rights with Filipinos, but this time even without any amendment to the present Constitution. Worse, movants’ interpretation opens up our national economy to effective control not only by Americans but also by all foreigners, be they Indonesians, Malaysians or Chinese, even in the absence of reciprocal treaty arrangements. At least the Parity Amendment, as implemented by the Laurel-Langley Agreement, gave the capital-starved Filipinos theoretical parity – the same rights as Americans to exploit natural resources, and to own and control public utilities, in the United States of America. Here, movants’ interpretation would effectively mean a unilateral opening up of our national economy to all foreigners, without any reciprocal arrangements. That would mean that Indonesians, Malaysians and Chinese nationals could effectively control our mining companies and public utilities while Filipinos, even if they have the capital, could not control similar corporations in these countries. … The 1935, 1973 and 1987 Constitutions have the same 60 percent Filipino ownership and control requirement for public utilities like PLOT. Any deviation from this requirement necessitates an amendment to the Constitution as exemplified by the Parity Amendment. This Court has no power to amend the Constitution for its power and duty is only to faithfully apply and interpret the Constitution.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A farmers' organization files a petition for prohibition directly with the Supreme Court to stop the government from bidding out several highway projects as one large package. It argues that the package creates a monopoly and shuts out smaller Filipino companies, that the bidders are "shady" companies without enough money, and that the matter is of transcendental importance. Proving these claims would require evidence about the bidders and the market. Based on GIOS-Samar v. DOTC, should the Court take the case?

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. The petition should be dismissed. The Court will not resolve a question that depends on factual issues, even if the case is said to be of transcendental importance. The petitioner should have gone first to the proper trial court or the Court of Appeals.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: The Supreme Court has original and concurrent jurisdiction with the RTC and the Court of Appeals over certiorari, prohibition, mandamus, quo warranto and habeas corpus. But under the doctrine of hierarchy of courts, direct recourse to the Court is proper only to seek the resolution of questions of law. The Court is not a trier of fact; it is not equipped, by structure or rule, to receive and evaluate evidence in the first instance. The doctrine is a constitutional filtering mechanism and a "bright-line rule which cannot be brushed aside by an invocation of the transcendental importance or constitutional dimension of the issue." The only case in which the Court may take up factual questions at the first instance is its constitutional task of reviewing the factual basis of a martial law proclamation (Section 18, Article VII).
suggestedAnswer.application: In GIOS-Samar, the petitioner's claims (monopoly, restraint of trade, shady bidders with shaky finances) were "inextricably intertwined with underlying questions of fact" needing evidence, for example about the relevant market, who is dominant, and the bidders' financial ability. The petitioner invoked transcendental importance, but the Court explained that the so-called special and important reasons are not what decides the matter; the nature of the question is. Because a factual issue was indispensable to the legal issue, the Court refused to resolve it.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The petition is dismissed; such a challenge must first be brought before the proper trial court or the Court of Appeals, which can try the facts.

keyPoints: Direct recourse to the Supreme Court is proper only for pure questions of law
The Court is not a trier of fact and cannot receive evidence in the first instance
Hierarchy of courts is a constitutional filtering mechanism and a bright-line rule
Transcendental importance cannot override the rule when a factual issue is indispensable
The only exception for factual questions: review of a martial law proclamation (Section 18, Article VII)
The case must first go to the proper trial court or the Court of Appeals

source.part: Decision, Part I (opening) and Part I-B (closing paragraph); Part II-G; Part II-I (final paragraphs)
source.excerpt: While petitioner asserts that the foregoing arguments involve legal (as opposed to factual) issues, our examination of the petition shows otherwise. As will be demonstrated shortly, petitioner's arguments against the constitutionality of the bundling of the Projects are inextricably intertwined with underlying questions of fact, the determination of which require the reception of evidence. This Court, however, is not a trier of fact. We cannot resolve these factual issues at the first instance. For this reason, we DISMISS the petition. … In fine, while this Court has original and concurrent jurisdiction with the RTC and the CA in the issuance of writs of certiorari, prohibition, mandamus, quo warranto, and habeas corpus (extraordinary writs), direct recourse to this Court is proper only to seek resolution of questions of law. Save for the single specific instance provided by the Constitution under Section 18, Article VII, cases the resolution of which depends on the determination of questions of fact cannot be brought directly before the Court because we are not a trier of facts. We are not equipped, either by structure or rule, to receive and evaluate evidence in the first instance; these are the primary functions of the lower courts or regulatory agencies. This is the raison d'etre behind the doctrine of hierarchy of courts. It operates as a constitutional filtering mechanism designed to enable this Court to focus on the more fundamental tasks assigned to it by the Constitution. It is a bright-line rule which cannot be brushed aside by an invocation of the transcendental importance or constitutional dimension of the issue or cause raised. … We take this opportunity to clarify that the presence of one or more of the so-called "special and important reasons" is not the decisive factor considered by the Court in deciding whether to permit the invocation, at the first instance, of its original jurisdiction over the issuance of extraordinary writs. Rather, it is the nature of the question raised by the parties in those "exceptions" that enabled us to allow the direct action before us. … To be clear, the transcendental importance doctrine does not clothe us with the power to tackle factual questions and play the role of a trial court. The only circumstance when we may take cognizance of a case in the first instance, despite the presence of factual issues, is in the exercise of our constitutionally-expressed task to review the sufficiency of the factual basis of the President's proclamation of martial law under Section 18, Article VII of the 1987 Constitution. The case before us does not fall under this exception. … Accordingly, for the guidance of the bench and the bar, we reiterate that when a question before the Court involves determination of a factual issue indispensable to the resolution of the legal issue, the Court will refuse to resolve the question regardless of the allegation or invocation of compelling reasons, such as the transcendental or paramount importance of the case. Such question must first be brought before the proper trial courts or the CA, both of which are specially equipped to try and resolve factual questions.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: The government awards an exclusive 30-year concession to build, operate and maintain several airports to the winning bidder in a public bidding. A critic says this creates a monopoly prohibited by Section 19, Article XII of the Constitution. Based on GIOS-Samar v. DOTC, is the critic correct? What does the Philippine Competition Act prohibit, and what would the critic have to prove?

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. A concession to a winning bidder does not by itself create a monopoly that violates the Constitution. A challenger would have to prove, with evidence, an abuse of a dominant position (or an anti-competitive agreement) under the Philippine Competition Act.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: The Constitution does not prohibit the operation of monopolies per se (Tatad v. Secretary of the Department of Energy). Certain public utilities or services must be given exclusive franchises if the public interest is to be served, and such exclusive franchises do not violate the law against monopolies (Anglo-Fil Trading Corporation v. Lazaro). The Constitution says the State may, by law, prohibit or regulate monopolies when the public interest so requires. The Philippine Competition Act (RA No. 10667) does not define a "monopoly"; it prohibits an entity that has achieved a "dominant position" in a "relevant market" from abusing it. An entity is not punished for simply securing a dominant position. The law also has built-in protections such as public bidding.
suggestedAnswer.application: In GIOS-Samar, the Court found that granting a concession for the exclusive development, operation and maintenance of the airports does not by itself create a monopoly violative of the Constitution, because exclusivity is inherent in a concession to deliver a public service. Whether a prohibited situation exists would need evidence that (1) the relevant market is airport development, maintenance and operation; (2) the entity has achieved a dominant position in it; and (3) the entity commits acts constituting abuse of that position. The petitioner also pointed to no law that prohibits the bundling of bids. The Court is not a trier of facts, so such a challenge should be brought before a tribunal equipped to resolve the factual and legal issues.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The critic is not correct that the concession alone is a prohibited monopoly; only an abuse of dominance proven by evidence would be punishable.

keyPoints: The Constitution does not prohibit monopolies per se
Exclusive franchises for public services are not violative of the law against monopolies
The State may prohibit or regulate monopolies by law when the public interest requires
The Competition Act (RA No. 10667) penalizes abuse of a dominant position, not merely having one
A challenger must prove the relevant market, dominance, and abusive conduct
Public bidding is a built-in protection

source.part: Decision, Part I-A (monopolies and combinations in restraint of trade)
source.excerpt: In Tatad v. Secretary of the Department of Energy, we clarified that the Constitution does not prohibit the operation of monopolies per se. With particular respect to the operation of public utilities or services, this Court, in Anglo-Fil Trading Corporation v. Lazaro, further clarified that "[b]y their very nature, certain public services or public utilities such as those which supply water, electricity, transportation, telephone, telegraph, etc. must be given exclusive franchises if public interest is to be served. Such exclusive franchises are not violative of the law against monopolies." … In short, we find that the grant of a concession agreement to an entity, as a winning bidder, for the exclusive development, operation, and maintenance of any or all of the Projects, does not by itself create a monopoly violative of the provisions of the Constitution. Anglo-Fil Trading Corporation teaches that exclusivity is inherent in the grant of a concession to a private entity to deliver a public service, where Government chooses not to undertake such service. Otherwise stated, while the grant may result in a monopoly, it is a type of monopoly not violative of law. This is the essence of the policy decision of the Government to enter into concessions with the private sector to build, maintain and operate what would have otherwise been government-operated services, such as airports. In any case, the law itself provides for built-in protections to safeguard the public interest, foremost of which is to require public bidding. Under the BOT Law, for example, a private-public pat1nership (PPP) agreement may be undertaken through public bidding, in cases of solicited proposals, or through "Swiss challenge" (also known as comparative bidding), in cases of unsolicited proposals. … RA No. 10667 does not define what constitutes a "monopoly." Instead, it prohibits one or more entities which has/have acquired or achieved a "dominant position" in a "relevant market" from "abusing" its dominant position. In other words, an entity is not prohibited from, or held liable for prosecution and punishment for, simply securing a dominant position in the relevant market in which it operates. It is only when that entity engages in conduct in abuse of its dominant position that it will be exposed to prosecution and possible punishment. … To illustrate, applying the facts and claims relative to the violation of the proscription against monopolies, what RA No. 10667, in fact, prohibits and punishes is the situation where: (1) an entity, having been granted an exclusive franchise to maintain and operate one or more airports, attains a dominant position in that market; and (2) abuses such dominant position by engaging in prohibited conduct, i.e., acts that substantially prevent, restrict or lessen competition in market of airport development, operations and maintenance. Thus, for petitioner to succeed in asserting that such a prohibited situation legally obtains, it must first establish, by evidence, that indeed: (1) the relevant market is that of airport development, maintenance, and operation (under the facts-based criteria enumerated in Section 24 of RA No. 10667); (2) the entity has achieved a dominant position (under the facts-based criteria enumerated in Section 27 of RA No. 10667) in that relevant market; and (3) the entity commits acts constituting abuse of dominant position (under the facts based criteria enumerated in Section 27 of RA No. 10667).

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A group says that the bidding for a government infrastructure project violates the Anti-Dummy Law and the 60% Filipino ownership rule for public utilities in Section 11, Article XII of the Constitution. It does not name any corporation that falsely pretended to have Filipino ownership, and it cites no law reserving the project to Filipino-owned corporations. Based on GIOS-Samar v. DOTC, how should these claims be decided?

suggestedAnswer.answer: The claims should be rejected. The petitioner failed to allege ultimate facts showing a violation of the Anti-Dummy Law, and, for the same reasons, the Section 11, Article XII claim fails too.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: For liability under Section 2 of the Anti-Dummy Law to attach, it must first be established that there is a law limiting or reserving the enjoyment of a right, franchise, privilege or business to Filipino citizens, or to corporations at least a certain percentage owned by them. It must also be shown by evidence that a corporation or association falsely simulated the existence of the minimum required Filipino stock or capital ownership. Executive Order No. 65 exempts contracts for infrastructure and development projects covered by the BOT Law from the 40% foreign ownership limitation.
suggestedAnswer.application: In GIOS-Samar, the petitioner did not identify any corporation or association that falsely simulated its stock ownership. It also did not allege any law limiting or requiring that infrastructure or development projects be awarded only to corporations a certain percentage of whose capital is owned by Filipinos. Since EO No. 65 even exempts BOT projects from the 40% foreign ownership limit, the Section 11, Article XII claim (a 60% Filipino ownership requirement for franchises and public utility operation) was rejected for the same reasons.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The anti-dummy and Section 11 claims fail for not alleging ultimate facts or a law reserving the project to Filipino-owned corporations.

keyPoints: Anti-Dummy Law: a law must limit the activity to Filipinos or Filipino-owned corporations
There must be evidence of falsely simulated Filipino ownership
The petitioner named no corporation that simulated ownership
EO No. 65 exempts BOT infrastructure contracts from the 40% foreign ownership limit
The Section 11, Article XII claim was rejected for the same reasons
The claims fail for not pleading ultimate facts (no cause of action)

source.part: Decision, Part I-B (anti-dummy law and Section 11, Article XII)
source.excerpt: For liability for violation of Section 2 to attach, it must first be established that there is a law limiting or reserving the enjoyment or exercise of a right, franchise, privilege, or business to citizens of the Philippines, or to corporations or associations at least a certain percentage of which is owned by such citizens. Moreover, it must be shown by evidence that a corporation or association falsely simulated the existence of the minimum required Filipino stock or capital ownership to enjoy or exercise the right, franchise, privilege, or business. … In this case, petitioner failed to allege ultimate facts showing how the bundling of the Projects violated the Anti-Dummy Law. It did not identify what corporation or association falsely simulated the composition of its stock ownership. Moreover, it did not allege that there is a law limiting, reserving, or requiring that infrastructure or development projects must be awarded only to corporations, a certain percentage of the capital of which is exclusively owned by Filipinos. Executive Order (EO) No. 65, even exempts contracts for infrastructure/development projects covered by the BOT Law from the 40% foreign ownership limitation. … For the same reasons above, petitioner's allegation that bundling violated Section 11, Article XII of the Constitution - which prescribes a 60% Filipino ownership requirement for franchises, certificate, or for the operation of public utilities - must be rejected.

questions.prompt: According to GIOS-Samar v. DOTC, what is the effect of invoking the "transcendental importance" of a case on the doctrine of hierarchy of courts?

choices.A: It lets the Court decide factual questions directly, whenever the issue is important enough
choices.B: It cannot override the doctrine, which is a bright-line rule, when a factual issue is indispensable to the resolution of the case
choices.C: It makes the doctrine optional for all constitutional issues
choices.D: It applies only to petitions filed by taxpayers

A is wrong because the Court said transcendental importance "does not clothe us with the power to tackle factual questions and play the role of a trial court." C is wrong because the Court said the doctrine is a constitutional imperative, not a matter of mere policy. D is wrong because the rule applies to any litigant seeking direct recourse.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: In GIOS-Samar v. DOTC, what is the only circumstance in which the Court may take up a case in the first instance despite the presence of factual issues?

choices.A: When the petitioner invokes transcendental importance
choices.B: When the petition is filed by a taxpayer
choices.C: When the Court reviews the sufficiency of the factual basis of the President's proclamation of martial law under Section 18, Article VII of the Constitution
choices.D: When the Solicitor General agrees to have the facts determined by the Court

questions.explanation: C is correct. The Court said: "The only circumstance when we may take cognizance of a case in the first instance, despite the presence of factual issues, is in the exercise of our constitutionally-expressed task to review the sufficiency of the factual basis of the President's proclamation of martial law under Section 18, Article VII of the 1987 Constitution." A is wrong because transcendental importance does not give the Court power to tackle factual questions. B is wrong because standing as a taxpayer does not change the rule. D is wrong because the parties' agreement is not an exception the Court recognized; the case before it did not fall under the exception.

source.part: Decision, Part II-G (exceptions to the doctrine of hierarchy of courts)
source.excerpt: To be clear, the transcendental importance doctrine does not clothe us with the power to tackle factual questions and play the role of a trial court. The only circumstance when we may take cognizance of a case in the first instance, despite the presence of factual issues, is in the exercise of our constitutionally-expressed task to review the sufficiency of the factual basis of the President's proclamation of martial law under Section 18, Article VII of the 1987 Constitution. The case before us does not fall under this exception.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: According to GIOS-Samar v. DOTC, strict observance of the doctrine of hierarchy of courts is a constitutional imperative because of which two considerations?

choices.A: The structure of the judicial system and the requirements of due process
choices.B: The size of the Court's budget and the number of its justices
choices.C: The separation of powers and the political question doctrine
choices.D: The need for speedy trial and the rule against forum shopping

questions.explanation: A is correct. The Court said strict observance of the doctrine "is a constitutional imperative given (1) the structure of our judicial system and (2) the requirements of due process." On structure, the doctrine recognizes the levels of courts and their roles: trial courts and the Court of Appeals can rule on facts, while the Supreme Court generally decides only questions of law. On due process, by going directly to the Court, litigants deprive themselves of the opportunity to completely pursue or defend their causes of action, because the Court cannot accept evidence in the first instance. B, C and D are not the reasons the Court gave.

source.part: Decision, Part II-H (hierarchy of courts is a constitutional imperative)
source.excerpt: Strict observance of the doctrine of hierarchy of courts should not be a matter of mere policy. It is a constitutional imperative given (1) the structure of our judicial system and (2) the requirements of due process. … Second. Strict adherence to the doctrine of hierarchy of courts also proceeds from considerations of due process. While the term "due process of law" evades exact and concrete definition, this Court, in one of its earliest decisions, referred to it as a law which hears before it condemns which proceeds upon inquiry and renders judgment only after trial. It means that every citizen shall hold his life, liberty, property, and immunities under the protection of the general rules which govern society. Under the present Rules of Court, which governs our judicial proceedings, warring factual allegations of parties are settled through presentation of evidence. Evidence is the means of ascertaining, in a judicial proceeding, the truth respecting a matter of fact: As earlier demonstrated, the Court cannot accept evidence in the first instance. By directly filing a case before the Court, litigants necessarily deprive themselves of the oportunity to completely pursue or defend their causes of actions. Their right to due process is effectively undermined by their own doing.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: In GIOS-Samar v. DOTC, which of the following is NOT one of the things the doctrine of hierarchy of courts operates to prevent?

choices.A: Inordinate demands upon the Court's time and attention which are better devoted to matters within its exclusive jurisdiction
choices.B: Further overcrowding of the Court's docket
choices.C: Delay in the adjudication of cases that must be remanded or referred to the lower court as the proper forum
choices.D: Any challenge to the constitutionality of a law, whatever the nature of the question

questions.explanation: D is correct because it is not one of the three things the Court listed, and the doctrine does not bar every constitutional challenge: direct recourse is allowed where the issue is one of law. The Court said the doctrine operates to (1) prevent inordinate demands upon the Court's time and attention which are better devoted to matters within its exclusive jurisdiction; (2) prevent further overcrowding of the Court's docket; and (3) prevent the resultant delay in the adjudication of cases which often have to be remanded or referred to the lower court as the proper forum under the rules of procedure, or as the court better equipped to resolve factual questions. A, B and C are the three listed purposes.

source.part: Decision, Part II-I (the doctrine of hierarchy of courts as a filtering mechanism)
source.excerpt: The doctrine of hierarchy of courts operates to: (1) prevent inordinate demands upon the Court's time and attention which are better devoted to those matters within its exclusive jurisdiction; (2) prevent further overcrowding of the Court's docket; and (3) prevent the inevitable and resultant delay, intended or otherwise, in the adjudication of cases which often have to be remanded or referred to the lower court as the proper forum under the rules of procedure, or as the court better equipped to resolve factual questions.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Which of the following is one of the four requisites for the exercise of the Court's power of judicial review mentioned in GIOS-Samar v. DOTC?

choices.A: The issue of constitutionality must be the very lis mota of the case
choices.B: The petitioner must be a member of Congress
choices.C: The law challenged must have been enacted within the past year
choices.D: The challenge must be filed with the Court of Appeals first, even if the question is purely legal

questions.explanation: A is correct. The four requisites are: (1) an actual case or controversy calling for the exercise of judicial power; (2) the person challenging the act must have standing, meaning a personal and substantial interest such that he has sustained, or will sustain, direct injury as a result of its enforcement; (3) the question of constitutionality must be raised at the earliest possible opportunity; and (4) the issue of constitutionality must be the very lis mota of the case. The Court added the further requirement that it can only resolve pure questions of law. B and C are not requirements. D is wrong because direct recourse to the Court is allowed when the question is purely one of law.

source.part: Decision, Part II-I (requisites of judicial review)
source.excerpt: As stated previously, parallel guidelines have been adopted by this Court in the exercise of judicial review: 1. actual case or controversy calling for the exercise of judicial power; 2. the person challenging the act must have "standing" to challenge; he must have a personal and substantial interest in the case such that he has sustained, or will sustain, direct injury as a result of its enforcement; 3. the question of constitutionality must be raised at the earliest possible opportunity; 4. the issue of constitutionality must be the very lis mota of the case. (Citations omitted.) Thus, the exercise of our power of judicial review is subject to these four requisites and the further requirement that we can only resolve pure questions of law.
